title: The question behind the question: IRAC and reframing
summary: A lawyer does not answer the question as asked; a lawyer finds the real issue under it, names the rule that decides it, applies the facts, and only then concludes. This lesson teaches that method, called IRAC, so your meetings with professionals start at the conditions instead of the question.
body:
Bottom line. A lawyer does not answer the question you asked. A lawyer finds the real issue under it, names the rule that decides it, applies the facts, and only then gives a conclusion. Learn to do that first step yourself, Mr Shabazz, and every meeting with a professional gets shorter and cheaper.

In plain English

When most people ask a legal question, they ask it as a yes-or-no. "Can I move my land into my company?" "Can I pay my brother from the Holdco?" A lawyer hears something different. A lawyer hears a bundle of smaller questions hiding inside the big one.

Here is a comparison. A doctor does not answer "can I run a marathon?" with yes or no. The doctor asks about your heart, your knees, and your training. Then the doctor answers a better question: "what would have to be true for a marathon to be safe for you?" Thinking like a lawyer is the same move.

The habit has four parts. Find the issue, the real thing in dispute or at risk. Find the rule, the law or contract term that decides it. Apply the rule to your exact facts. Then conclude. Lawyers call this IRAC. It is the oldest tool in legal training, and it works for business decisions too.

The framework

IRAC stands for Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion. Run it in that order, every time.

  1. Issue. Rewrite the question so it names what is actually at stake. "Can I transfer the land?" becomes "What does a transfer trigger: tax, fees, consents, and who must agree?"
  2. Rule. Name the source that decides each piece. A statute, which is a law passed by a legislature. A regulation, a contract clause, a bank covenant, a trust deed. If you do not know the source, that is your first task, not a reason to guess.
  3. Application. Put your real facts against the rule. Not the facts you wish you had. The land is in one name, the company may not yet exist, the bank may hold a charge, which is a registered claim against the land. Each fact changes the answer.
  4. Conclusion. Now give the answer, with its conditions attached. "Yes, if the company exists, if the lender consents, and if the tax cost is acceptable." A conclusion without conditions is a guess.

Add one more question that lawyers ask by reflex: who has the power to decide this? A regulator, a lender, a co-owner, a trustee, a court. If the answer is "someone other than me", your real task is to satisfy that person, not to convince yourself.

A worked example

Hypothetical. A developer owns a building lot in her own name. She asks: "Can I just put the land into my new company?"

Issue. The real issues are: does the company exist yet; what does the transfer cost in tax and government fees; does any lender or co-owner have to agree; and does moving the land change who the regulator thinks is the owner.

Rule. Four different sources decide those four issues: company law for existence, tax law for the cost, the mortgage document for consent, and the planning authority's own rules for ownership. One question, four rulebooks.

Application. Suppose the company is not yet registered. Then the answer to the whole question is "not yet", whatever the tax rules say. Suppose it is registered, but a bank holds a mortgage that says "no transfer without our written consent". Then the next step is a letter to the bank, not a deed.

Conclusion. "Yes, once the company exists, with the bank's written consent, after a tax professional has priced the transfer in both countries." Notice that the conclusion is a sequence of steps, not a word.

Professional Sign-Off Required: real estate counsel in the land's jurisdiction, and a tax advisor in each country involved, before any transfer document is signed.

The beginner mistake

Accepting the question as it was asked. A yes-or-no question invites a yes-or-no answer, and a yes-or-no answer hides every condition that matters. The second mistake follows from the first: acting on the "yes" before anyone checked the conditions. Most expensive legal problems start with a true "yes" that was missing three "ifs".

How you will use it

As a developer, you face questions like this every week. Can we start site work before the permit? Can the company pay this invoice for my other business? Can we sign this offer today? Each one is an IRAC question in disguise.

Use the method in three places. First, before you call a lawyer or accountant: write the issue and the list of rulebooks on one page, so the professional spends the paid hour on your conditions, not on working out what you meant. Second, when a team member brings you a "yes": ask them for the "if" list behind it. Third, when you read a contract or a lender's letter: find the clause that decides your issue before you form an opinion.

The result is not that you become your own lawyer. The result is that you arrive with the right question, and you can tell when an answer is missing its conditions.
checklist: Rewrite the question so it names what is at risk.
List every rulebook that touches it. Expect more than one.
Write your real facts down. Mark each one: known, assumed, or unverified.
Ask who has the power to decide. Plan to satisfy that person.
State the conclusion as "yes, if" with every condition listed.
Name which licensed professional must sign off before you act.

selftest.q: A friend asks you: "Can my company lend me money to buy a house?" Before you answer, write the four IRAC lines.
selftest.a: Issue: not "can it lend" but "what does a loan from a company to its owner trigger: tax on the owner, rules on repayment timing, and what the company's own documents allow." Rule: tax law on shareholder loans, the company's articles and any shareholder agreement, and any bank covenant that limits related-party loans [specific rules unverified — confirm independently]. Application: it depends on the repayment period, whether interest is charged, and whether the company's lender must consent. Conclusion: "Possibly, if it is repaid within the period the tax rules allow, documented as a real loan, and not blocked by the bank." Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor.

apply: Take one live question on your desk this week. Write it the way you first thought it. Under it, write the IRAC version: the issue, the rulebooks, your facts marked known or unverified, and a "yes, if" conclusion. Bring that page to your next professional meeting. You will spend the meeting on the conditions, not on the question.
sources: IRAC is a standard method taught in common-law legal education. This lesson teaches the method only. It cites no statute and gives no jurisdiction-specific advice. Seed video: Greg Baker on the At The Top podcast, who, as reported, represented himself at Australia's Fair Work Commission with AI agents and won (Baker v Macquarie University [2026] FWC 3054, 12 August 2026, as reported in Australian legal press). His case is the long argument for this lesson's habit: where the facts and the law both live in writing, a prepared non-lawyer who frames the issue correctly can defend a position on paper. The university was reported to be considering an appeal. Read the decision itself before quoting its reasoning. Figures in the example are hypothetical. Education only.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: real estate counsel in the land's jurisdiction, and a tax advisor in each country involved, before any transfer document is signed.

title: Facts first: fact, assumption, inference, conclusion
summary: Most expensive mistakes start with a statement that was treated as a fact but was never proved. This lesson teaches you to sort every statement into fact, assumption, inference or conclusion, and to check the assumption that moves the most money first.
body:
Bottom line. Most mistakes come from a "fact" that was never a fact. Before you decide anything, sort every statement into one of four boxes: fact, assumption, inference, or conclusion. Then check the assumption that moves the most money first.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, think about the last deal meeting you sat in. Someone said "the seller owns it outright". Someone else said "the zoning allows four units". A third person said "we can close in a month". All three sentences sounded the same. They were said in the same calm voice, around the same table. But they were not the same kind of statement at all.

The first may be true, but nobody had checked the title. The second was a belief that nobody had confirmed in writing. The third was a prediction built on the first two. Lawyers are trained to hear that difference. Most business people are not, and that is where money is lost.

Courts work this way. A judge does not care how sure a witness felt. A judge asks what the evidence proves. You can bring the same discipline to your own decisions, long before anything reaches a court.

The framework

Every statement in a decision belongs in one of four boxes.

  1. Fact. A statement you can prove with a document, a public record, or a witness who saw it. A title search result is a fact. A signed letter from the city is a fact. Every fact carries two labels: its source and its date. A fact from last year may not be a fact today.
  2. Assumption. A statement you believe but have not checked. "The seller owns it" is an assumption until you have the title search. Assumptions are normal and useful. The danger is forgetting that they are assumptions. Every assumption carries two labels: an owner, meaning the person who will check it, and a check, meaning the document that would turn it into a fact.
  3. Inference. A reasoning step that goes from facts to something new. "The title is clean and the buyer has financing, so we can close in thirty days" is an inference. An inference is only as good as the facts under it and the logic between them.
  4. Conclusion. The decision you reach at the end. Here is the key rule: a conclusion inherits the weakness of its weakest box. If one assumption under it is wrong, the whole conclusion is wrong, however strong the rest is.

Then rank your assumptions. Do not check them in the order they were said. Check first the assumption that would move the most money if it turned out to be false.

A worked example

Hypothetical. A developer is offered a building lot for 400,000. The plan is four townhouse units. Three statements are on the table.

  • "The seller owns it outright." This is an assumption until a title search confirms the owner and shows no mortgage, lien or caveat against the land.
  • "The zoning allows four units." This is an assumption until the planning authority confirms it in writing for this specific lot.
  • "We can close in thirty days." This is an inference that depends on both of the above.

Now rank the assumptions by money. Suppose the finished value is about 150,000 per unit of land value once approved. Four units gives 600,000. If the zoning allows only two units, the value falls to 300,000. That one assumption carries 300,000 of value, and it can be tested with a one-page letter from the planning office. Check it first. The title search is also essential, but here it protects the 400,000 price rather than a swing in value.

The conclusion is now written honestly: "Yes, buy at 400,000, if the title search is clean and if the city confirms four units in writing before the deposit becomes non-refundable."

Professional Sign-Off Required: real estate counsel for the title; a planning professional for the zoning.

The beginner mistake

Treating a confident tone as proof. The person who sounds most certain is often the person who checked least. A related mistake is writing assumptions in the same style as facts, in the same list, in the same font. Once an assumption is typed into a slide as a plain sentence, everyone in the room starts to treat it as a fact, including the person who wrote it.

How you will use it

Use the four boxes on any document that drives a decision: an investment memo, a lender package, a site report, a note from a broker. Go through it line by line and mark each sentence F, A, I or C. You will usually find that the most important sentences are assumptions.

Then give each assumption an owner and a deadline. "Planning letter, owner: project manager, due Friday." When the letter arrives, move that line into the fact box, with its source and date. Your conclusion becomes stronger one box at a time, and you can show a lender or a partner exactly what has been proved and what has not.
checklist: List every statement the decision depends on.
Label each one: fact, assumption, inference or conclusion.
Give every fact a source and a date.
Give every assumption an owner, a check and a deadline.
Check first the assumption that moves the most money.
Write the conclusion as "yes, if" with the open assumptions as conditions.

selftest.q: Someone tells you: "My company can lend me 50,000. My accountant said it was fine last year, and the shareholders will not mind." Sort these statements into the four boxes.
selftest.a: "My accountant said it was fine last year" is a remembered statement about a different time and possibly a different loan, so it is an assumption until the accountant confirms it in writing for this loan. "The shareholders will not mind" is a prediction, which is also an assumption; the check is a signed shareholder or director resolution. "My company can lend me 50,000" is a conclusion, and it rests on both of those unchecked assumptions, so it is no stronger than them. Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor.

apply: Draw a line down the middle of a page. On the left, write "What I know" and list each item with its source and date. On the right, write "What I am assuming" and list each item with the name of the person who will check it and the document that would prove it. Do this for one live deal.
sources: This lesson teaches a reasoning method only. It cites no statute and gives no jurisdiction-specific advice. The distinction between evidence and belief is standard in common-law legal training. All figures are hypothetical. Education only.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: real estate counsel for the title; a planning professional for the zoning.

title: Reading a rule: elements, exceptions, burdens
summary: Every rule, whether in a statute or a contract, can be broken into elements that must all be met, exceptions that switch it off, and a burden that says who must prove what. Reading a rule this way tells you exactly which facts you need to collect.
body:
Bottom line. A rule is not a sentence to be read once. It is a list of tests. Break every rule into its elements, its exceptions, and its burdens, and you will know exactly which facts you must prove and which the other side must prove.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, when you read a building code, you do not read it as a story. You read it as a set of requirements: this width, this height, this fire rating. If one requirement fails, the design fails. Legal rules work the same way, but they are written in long sentences that hide the list.

A lawyer's first job with any rule is to turn the sentence back into a list. The list has three parts. The elements are the conditions that must all be true for the rule to apply. The exceptions are the situations where the rule does not apply even if every element is met. The burden is the question of who has to prove each part, and how strongly.

Once you see a rule this way, an argument stops being a contest of opinions. It becomes a question of which items on the list are proved.

The framework

  1. Find the trigger and the result. Every rule says "if these things happen, then this follows". Write down the result first, so you know what is at stake.
  2. List the elements. Split the "if" part at every "and". Each piece is a separate element. All of them must be met. Watch the small words. "And" means every item is required. "Or" means any one is enough. "Within", "before" and "after" are time elements and are often the easiest to prove or disprove.
  3. List the exceptions. Look for "unless", "except", "provided that", "other than" and "subject to". Each one opens a door that can switch the rule off.
  4. Read the verbs. "Shall" or "must" usually creates an obligation. "May" usually gives a choice, not a duty. A choice can be left unused.
  5. Assign the burden. As a general concept in civil disputes, the person relying on a rule must prove its elements, and the person relying on an exception must usually prove the exception. The standard in most civil matters is the balance of probabilities, which means "more likely than not". Contracts can change who proves what, so read for that too.
  6. Match facts to each line. Next to each element and exception, write the fact and the document that proves it, or write "missing".

A worked example

Hypothetical. A purchase agreement for land says: "The Buyer may terminate this Agreement and recover the Deposit if the Seller fails to deliver a title search showing no registered charges within 30 days after the Deposit is paid, unless the delay is caused by the land titles office."

The deposit is 50,000. Here is the rule broken into its parts.

  • Result: the buyer may end the deal and get the 50,000 back.
  • Element 1: the seller did not deliver a title search.
  • Element 2: the search had to show no registered charges.
  • Element 3: the 30 days are counted from the date the deposit was paid, not from the signing date.
  • Exception: the delay was caused by the land titles office.
  • Verb: "may". The buyer has a choice. If the buyer does nothing, the deal continues.

Now the burden. The buyer, relying on the rule, should be ready to prove the deposit date and that no clean search arrived in time. The seller, relying on the exception, should be ready to prove the office caused the delay. Each side now knows exactly which documents to gather: a bank record of the deposit, the email history, and any notice from the land titles office.

Professional Sign-Off Required: real estate counsel before any termination notice is sent.

The beginner mistake

Reading for the general idea instead of the exact words. People remember a clause as "we can walk away if the title is bad". The real clause may say "within 30 days after the deposit", and the buyer may already be on day 34. A second mistake is ignoring the exception because it is at the end of the sentence. The exception is often where the other side will build its whole case.

How you will use it

Use this method on any clause that controls money or time. A financing condition. A lender covenant that lets the bank call the loan. A permit rule with a deadline. A termination right in a construction contract.

Write the clause as a short table: result, elements, exceptions, verb, who proves what. Then fill in the facts column. A gap in the facts column is your to-do list. A gap you cannot fill is a question for your lawyer, and now it is a precise question, not a general worry.
checklist: Write the result of the rule first.
Split the conditions at every "and" and "or".
Find every "unless", "except", "provided that" and "subject to".
Check whether the verb is "shall" or "may".
Note who must prove each element and each exception.
Put a fact and a document next to every line, or write "missing".

selftest.q: A lease says: "The Tenant may assign this Lease with the Landlord's consent, which shall not be unreasonably withheld, except to a competitor of the Landlord." Break it into result, elements, exception, verb and burden.
selftest.a: Result: the tenant may assign, meaning transfer, the lease. Elements: the tenant asks for consent, and the landlord gives it. Built-in limit on the landlord: consent cannot be unreasonably withheld, so a refusal must have a reasonable basis. Exception: the assignee is a competitor of the landlord, and in that case the landlord may refuse freely. Verbs: "may" gives the tenant a choice; "shall not" puts a duty on the landlord. Burden, as a general concept: the tenant relying on the duty should be ready to show the refusal was unreasonable; the landlord relying on the exception should be ready to show the assignee is a competitor. Professional Sign-Off Required: commercial leasing counsel.

apply: Pick one clause from a contract you have signed or are about to sign that controls money or a deadline. Rewrite it as a table with these rows: result, each element, each exception, the verb, and who proves what. Fill in the facts column and circle every gap.
sources: This lesson teaches a reading method. The description of burdens and the balance of probabilities is a general common-law concept, not a statement of any specific statute; how burdens apply in a given dispute depends on the jurisdiction and the contract [confirm independently with counsel]. Clause wording and figures are hypothetical. Education only.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: real estate counsel before any termination notice is sent.

title: Risk thinking: worst case, probability, reversibility, one-way doors
summary: Lawyers rank risks by how bad the worst case is, how likely it is, and whether it can be undone. This lesson teaches you to spend your care and your professional fees on the decisions you cannot reverse.
body:
Bottom line. Not every risk deserves the same care. Rank each decision by the worst case, the probability, and whether you can undo it. Move fast on decisions you can reverse. Slow down and pay for advice on the ones you cannot.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, a good lawyer is sometimes described as a professional pessimist. That is not because lawyers expect the worst. It is because their job is to ask "what is the worst thing that could happen here, and could we survive it?" before anyone signs.

Business people often ask a different question: "how likely is this to go wrong?" Both questions matter. A risk that is unlikely but would end the company deserves more attention than a risk that is likely but small.

There is a third question that experienced decision makers add: can I undo this? Some decisions are like a door you can walk back through. Others are like a door that locks behind you. People in business call these one-way doors. A one-way door is a decision that is costly or impossible to reverse once made. Signing a personal guarantee is a one-way door. Choosing a meeting time is not.

The framework

  1. Worst case. Describe the realistic worst outcome in plain words and put a number on it. "We lose the 20,000 deposit" is clear. "Things could go badly" is not.
  2. Probability. Estimate how likely the worst case is. You do not need precision. Low, medium and high is enough to start.
  3. Expected cost. Multiply the size of the loss by the probability. A 10 percent chance of losing 100,000 has an expected cost of 10,000. This helps you compare risks of different shapes.
  4. Reversibility. Ask: if this goes wrong, can I undo it, and at what cost? A notice can often be withdrawn. A registered transfer of land, a signed guarantee or a missed limitation period usually cannot.
  5. Survivability. Ask whether the worst case would end the business or your personal finances. If it would, no low probability makes it acceptable without protection.
  6. Decide the level of care. Reversible and small: decide quickly yourself. Reversible but large: get a second opinion. Irreversible: get professional sign-off before you act.

A worked example

Hypothetical. A developer must make two decisions this week.

Decision A: pay a 10,000 non-refundable fee for a 90-day option to buy a lot. Worst case: lose 10,000. Probability: medium. Expected cost: about 5,000. Survivable: yes. Reversible: the money is gone, but the developer is not bound to buy. This is a two-way door with a capped cost. Decide quickly.

Decision B: personally guarantee a 1,000,000 construction loan to the company. Worst case: the project fails and the bank pursues the developer's personal assets for the shortfall, say 400,000. Probability: low, perhaps 5 percent. Expected cost: 20,000. That number looks small. But the worst case may not be survivable, and once signed, the guarantee usually cannot be withdrawn without the bank's agreement. This is a one-way door.

On expected cost alone, B looks about four times as serious as A. Reversibility and survivability show it is in a different class. B deserves a lawyer's review of the guarantee terms, a cap on the amount if the bank will accept one, and a clear end date.

Professional Sign-Off Required: independent legal counsel for the guarantor before the guarantee is signed.

The beginner mistake

Treating every decision with the same level of care. Some people agonise over small, reversible choices and then sign a guarantee in five minutes because the bank needs it today. Another common mistake is relying only on probability. "It is very unlikely" is not an answer when the worst case cannot be survived. A third mistake is forgetting time. Many rights expire if you do nothing, so doing nothing can itself be a one-way door.

How you will use it

Keep a short list of your own one-way doors: signing guarantees, transferring land, issuing shares, giving up a deadline or a right in writing, and filing anything with a court or tribunal. When one of these comes up, stop and get sign-off.

For reversible decisions, act and learn. This is also how to decide what you can prepare yourself and what you must hand to a professional. As reported, Greg Baker represented himself at the Fair Work Commission and won, in a matter where the facts and the law were mostly in writing. That kind of preparation work is often a two-way door. The final signature on a binding document is not.

Finally, write the risk ranking down and keep it with the deal file. When a partner, a lender or a lawyer asks why you moved quickly on one item and slowly on another, the page answers for you. It also shows you, months later, whether your probability estimates were sensible, which is how your judgment improves over time.
checklist: Write the realistic worst case in one sentence with a number.
Estimate the probability: low, medium or high.
Multiply size by probability to compare risks.
Ask whether the decision can be undone, and at what cost.
Ask whether the worst case is survivable.
Keep a list of your own one-way doors and stop at each one.

selftest.q: A contractor offers a 5 percent discount if you sign today and waive your right to a holdback on the contract. Apply the four questions.
selftest.a: Worst case: the contractor leaves defects or fails to pay subcontractors, and you have no money held back to cover them; the loss could be far larger than the discount. Probability: unknown without checking the contractor, so treat it as medium. Reversibility: a written waiver of a right is usually hard or impossible to undo, so this is a one-way door. Survivability: depends on the contract size. Conclusion: do not decide today; the discount is a reason to slow down, not to speed up. Holdback rules are set by statute in many places and may not be waivable at all [unverified — confirm independently]. Professional Sign-Off Required: construction counsel.

apply: List five decisions you expect to make in the next month. For each, write the worst case with a number, the probability, and whether it can be undone. Mark every one-way door and note which professional must review it before you act.
sources: This lesson teaches a risk method. Expected cost as probability times impact is a standard decision-analysis concept. The one-way door idea is a common business metaphor, not a legal rule. The reference to Greg Baker is as reported: Baker v Macquarie University [2026] FWC 3054, 12 August 2026, reported in Australian legal press; the university was reported to be considering an appeal. The holdback point in the self-test is tagged unverified. All figures are hypothetical. Education only.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: independent legal counsel for the guarantor before the guarantee is signed.
